title: Polyprotic Acids
lead: Some acids hold more than one ionizable hydrogen atom, as carbonic acid and phosphoric acid do, and give them up to water one proton at a time, each step with an ionization constant of its own; some bases, such as the carbonate ion, accept more than one proton in the same stepwise way.
objectives: Extend previously introduced equilibrium concepts to acids and bases that may donate or accept more than one proton
summary_html: An acid that contains more than one ionizable proton is a polyprotic acid. These acids undergo stepwise ionization reactions involving the transfer of single protons. The ionization constants for polyprotic acids decrease with each subsequent step; these decreases typically are large enough to permit simple equilibrium calculations that treat each step separately.
notes: Nothing of the section is left out; the ICE table of Example 14.19 is written as a table, the acetic acid equation is kept as the book’s image, and the example’s closing line keeps its [H₃O⁺] = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ without a unit, as printed.

The two unkeyed numerical exercises are left out, and no answer is computed for them: fs-idp108710816 and fs-idp33679104. The keyed exercise fs-idm75310368 (exercise 64, nicotine as a base that accepts two protons) is printed in 14.3 and placed here, where polyprotic bases are taught. Numeric answers accept 2%, except the one-significant-figure concentrations of the Check Your Learning and of exercise 64, which accept 10%.

exercises.prompt:
The concentration of H2S in a saturated aqueous solution at room temperature is approximately 0.1 M. Calculate $[{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}],$ [HS−], and [S2−] in the solution:
${\text{H}}_{2}\text{S}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{HS}}^{-}(aq)\hspace{5em}{K}_{\text{a}1}=8.9\;\times\;{10}^{-8}$
${\text{HS}}^{-}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{S}}^{2-}(aq)\hspace{5em}{K}_{\text{a}2}=1.0\;\times\;{10}^{-19}$

parts.hint: Treat the first ionization alone with an ICE table, as in Example 14.19, assuming x is small beside 0.1.
Put the [H₃O⁺] and [HS⁻] of the first step into the expression for the second ionization.

exercises.prompt: Nicotine, C10H14N2, is a base that will accept two protons (Kb1 = 7 × 10−7, Kb2 = 1.4 × 10−11). What is the concentration of each species present in a 0.050-M solution of nicotine?

parts.hint: Treat the first step, the base ionization with K_b1, alone with an ICE table, as a polyprotic acid is treated.
The second step's product comes from K_b2 with the [C₁₀H₁₄N₂H⁺] and [OH⁻] of the first step.
Use the ion-product constant for water with [OH⁻].

exercises.prompt: Which of the following concentrations would be practically equal in a calculation of the equilibrium concentrations in a 0.134-M solution of H2CO3, a diprotic acid: $[{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}],$ [OH−], [H2CO3], $[{\text{HCO}}_{3}{}^{-}],$ $[{\text{CO}}_{3}{}^{2-}]?$ No calculations are needed to answer this question.

Calculate the concentration of each species present in a 0.010-M solution of phthalic acid, C6H4(CO2H)2.
$\begin{array}{l}{\text{C}}_{6}{\text{H}}_{4}{({\text{CO}}_{2}\text{H})}_{2}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{C}}_{6}{\text{H}}_{4}({\text{CO}}_{2}\text{H})\;{({\text{CO}}_{2})}^{-}(aq)\hspace{4em}{K}_{\text{a}}=1.1\;\times\;{10}^{-3} \\ {\text{C}}_{6}{\text{H}}_{4}({\text{CO}}_{2}\text{H})({\text{CO}}_{2}){}^{-}\;(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{C}}_{6}{\text{H}}_{4}{({\text{CO}}_{2})}_{2}{}^{2-}(aq)\hspace{5em}{K}_{\text{a}}=3.9\;\times\;{10}^{-6}\end{array}$

parts.hint: K_a1 is too large beside 0.010 to neglect x, so solve the first step's quadratic.
With the first step's two equal concentrations in the second ionization's expression, they cancel.

exercises.prompt:
The ion HTe− is an amphiprotic species; it can act as either an acid or a base.
(a) What is Ka for the acid reaction of HTe− with H2O?
(b) What is Kb for the reaction in which HTe− functions as a base in water?
(c) Demonstrate whether or not the second ionization of H2Te can be neglected in the calculation of [HTe−] in a 0.10 M solution of H2Te.

parts.hint: The acid reaction of HTe⁻ is the second ionization of H₂Te; look up its constant in Appendix H.
HTe⁻ acting as a base is the conjugate base of H₂Te, so divide K_w by the first ionization constant of H₂Te.

answer.solution:
(a) ${K}_{\text{a2}}=1.5\;\times\;{10}^{-11};$
(b) ${K}_{\text{b}}=4.3\;\times\;{10}^{-12};$
(c) $\frac{[{\text{Te}}^{2-}][{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}]}{[{\text{HTe}}^{-}]}=\frac{(x)(0.0141+x)}{(0.0141-x)}\approx\frac{(x)(0.0141)}{0.0141}=1.5\;\times\;{10}^{-11}$
Solving for x gives 1.5 × 10−11 M. Therefore, compared with 0.014 M, this value is negligible (1.1 × 10−7%).
